pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 5–7 — explore rock pools (tide pools) as small ocean habitats where crabs, anemones, starfish and small fish live, and that these creatures are adapted to survive crashing waves and changing water levels.
• Standards — UK (DfE KS1): Y2 'identify and name a variety of plants and animals in their habitats, including micro-habitats' and 'identify that most living things live in habitats to which they are suited' — the rock pool is a classic KS1 micro-habitat study.
• Standards — US (NGSS): K-ESS3-1 / 2-LS4-1 — organisms live where their needs are met; compare life in a specific habitat; early structure-for-survival ideas.
• Operational details: two goals — (1) NAME residents of a rock pool (crab, anemone, starfish, limpet, small fish, shrimp); (2) grasp ONE coping adaptation for the pool's harsh, changing conditions (limpet clamps to rock against waves; crab hides in a crevice; anemone pulls in its tentacles / holds water when the tide goes out). Keep adaptation concrete and singular; the deeper adaptation topic is the 7–9 dependent. Encourage a 'look closely, don't disturb' observational stance.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~5–6): names ≥3 rock-pool creatures and calls the pool a little sea home; Tier B (~6–7): describes it as a habitat left behind by the tide and names one animal's home; Tier C (~7): explains one way an animal copes with waves/changing water (limpet clamps down; anemone holds water).
bestPractices: Frame the rock pool as a micro-habitat 'left behind when the tide goes out' — connect to the coasts/tides prior knowledge so the changing water level makes sense.
Prioritise close observation: real photos/video of a crab scuttling, an anemone's tentacles waving then retracting — the behaviours ARE the adaptation evidence.
Teach one clear coping strategy per animal (limpet clamps, crab hides, anemone withdraws) rather than a list — concrete cause–effect the child can act out.
Model a 'gentle scientist' stance (look, don't grab; put creatures back) — habits of careful field observation.
Use a 'find the hidden creatures' game — rock-pool animals are camouflaged/tucked away, so searching mirrors real rock-pooling and rewards attention.
keyRepresentations: A top-down rock-pool scene with creatures tucked in crevices and under weed to find
Before/after tide panels: pool full at high tide vs exposed at low tide (why conditions change)
A limpet-clamping / anemone-retracting mini animation showing one coping behaviour
Resident ID cards (crab, anemone, starfish, limpet, blenny, shrimp) with 'where it hides'
commonMisconceptions: 'A rock pool is just a puddle' — not seeing it as a living habitat full of animals.
'The animals are stuck there by accident' — missing that they are suited to and survive the pool's harsh, changing conditions.
'An anemone is a plant/flower' — it's an animal (the waving 'petals' are tentacles).
'Starfish are fish' — they are invertebrates (seeds the later classifying topic).
'Nothing lives in a rock pool when the tide is out' — not grasping that animals cope (clamp down, hide, hold water) until the sea returns.

learn.summary: For ages 5–7: explore a rock pool (tide pool) as a small ocean habitat on the shore where crabs, anemones, starfish, limpets, small fish and shrimp live, and grasp ONE concrete way an animal copes with crashing waves and changing water levels. Two learning goals: (1) name at least three rock-pool residents and recognise the pool as a little sea home; (2) describe one coping adaptation (limpet clamps to rock; anemone pulls in tentacles/holds water; crab hides in a crevice). Keep the adaptation concrete and singular — deeper adaptation study belongs to a later age. Foster a 'look closely, don't disturb' observational stance. Aligns with UK KS1 Y2 living-things-and-habitats and NGSS K-ESS3-1 / 2-LS4-1 as a classic micro-habitat study.

activities.title: Peer into the pool and find the hidden creatures
feedback: When a creature is found, confirm its name and show it in its hiding spot: 'Yes — that's a crab, tucked into the crack in the rock.'
If the learner thinks the anemone is a plant/flower, point out the waving 'petals' are tentacles — it is an animal.
If the learner calls the starfish a fish, note gently that a starfish is not a fish — it's a different kind of sea animal (we sort animals into groups more carefully in a later topic).

When the tide drops, narrate the coping move: 'See — the limpet on the bare rock clamps flat to keep water in, and an anemone left out of the water balls up so it doesn't dry out until the sea comes back.'
Reinforce the big idea: the sea went out, but the pool still holds seawater and the animals are still there and alive — this is their home.
activities.rationale: Real rock-pooling is a look-closely, spot-and-identify activity; searching mirrors that because the animals are camouflaged and tucked away, rewarding careful attention. A high-tide/low-tide view makes visible WHY conditions change and lets the child link the real coping behaviours (clamping, retracting) to the changing water level — matching the naming + one-adaptation goal for this age.
sourceClaims: Rock-pool (intertidal) animals are adapted to survive wave action and changing water levels — e.g. limpets clamp tightly to rock and anemones retract their tentacles/retain water when exposed at low tide.
learnerActions: Study a detailed top-down picture of a rock pool where creatures are tucked under seaweed and in crevices, as they really are when you go rock-pooling.
Search for and point to each hidden animal (crab, anemone, starfish, limpet, small fish/blenny, shrimp) — reveal each one and learn its name.
For each creature found, uncover 'how it copes' with pool life: the limpet clamps tightly to the rock against the waves; the anemone pulls in its waving tentacles; the crab tucks under a ledge.

Change the water level from high tide (the pool covered by the sea) to low tide (the sea goes out, the rocks around the pool are uncovered, and the pool is left holding less seawater). Watch which animals clamp down, ball up, or hide away, and notice that the pool still holds seawater and is still full of life.
activities.intendedInsight: A rock pool is not just a puddle — it is a small, tough ocean home that changes as the tide comes and goes, and every animal has its own trick for surviving the waves and the sea going out.

activities.title: Help each animal survive the changing tide
feedback: When the right coping move is made in time, confirm the cause–effect: 'You clamped the limpet down — the wave couldn't wash it away.'
If a move is missed or wrong, show the gentle consequence and retry: 'The limpet was still loose, so the wave swept it off — try clamping it before the next wave.'
Connect action to the idea: 'That's how the real animal copes with the pool's crashing waves.'
activities.rationale: Performing the coping move with immediate cause–effect may make the adaptation felt through action rather than told as a fact, and acting it out with the body gives a concrete, memorable anchor. This reaches the explain-one-coping-strategy goal, slightly beyond the minimum for this age, so treat it as an extension of the naming activity. The coping behaviours themselves (limpet clamping, anemone retraction) are grounded in the cited shore biology, but the efficacy of this interaction format is untested.
sourceClaims: Rock-pool (intertidal) animals are adapted to survive wave action and changing water levels — e.g. limpets clamp tightly to rock and anemones retract their tentacles/retain water when exposed at low tide.
learnerActions: Watch or control a wave crashing in / the tide dropping out over the pool.
Perform each animal's coping move in time with the change: clamp the limpet flat to the rock, hide the crab under a ledge, pull in the anemone's tentacles.
Notice the consequence: if the limpet is left loose when a wave crashes, it gets swept away — if it clamps down, it stays safe.
Act out the moves with your own body too — clamp like a limpet, close up like an anemone, scuttle and hide like a crab.
activities.intendedInsight: The way an animal copes is an action with a reason: clamping, hiding and closing up are what keep these creatures safe when waves crash and the water drops — being 'adapted' means being built for these changes.

activities.title: Is the crab trapped? Talk it through
feedback: Target answer to model and build toward: a rock pool is a small ocean habitat the animals are suited to; when waves crash and the tide changes, crabs scuttle under rocks or into cracks, anemones pull in their tentacles and close up so they don't dry out, and limpets clamp down tightly.

If the learner says the animals are stuck/dying and wants to 'rescue' them, reframe the pool as their HOME, not a trap — show one coping behaviour (a closed-up anemone) to replace the pity story with adaptation.

If the learner treats the pool as a still, unchanging tank, explain the tide covers and uncovers the pool (about twice a day on most shores) — sometimes crashing waves, sometimes exposed — and the animals are adapted to those big changes.

If the learner can name creatures but not say how any copes, take one named animal and act out its move (clamp like a limpet, close like an anemone, hide like a crab), attaching a coping action to each creature.
Reinforce the 'gentle scientist' stance: because the rock pool is the animals' home, we look and don't grab, and we put creatures back.
activities.rationale: A two-tier contrast (name the habitat, then explain how an animal copes) is intended to discriminate a child who grasps adaptation from one holding the 'stranded and struggling' misconception: only the former can supply a real coping behaviour rather than sympathy. Discussing it aloud can surface the reasoning and the tide link. Spoken dialogue is offered as a supplement here; naming and the coping idea may be more reliably anchored visually/by action first for this age (a design proposal, not a source-established ranking), since recognition in talk alone does not guarantee independent naming.
learnerActions: Consider the claim: 'A child finds a crab and an anemone in a rock pool and says — they're trapped here, the sea left them behind, so they must be stuck and struggling. Is that right?'
Say in your own words what a rock pool is (a small ocean home, not a trap), and explain how an animal copes when waves crash and the water goes up and down.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'When a big wave crashes, what does the crab do? What does the anemone do?'; 'What makes the water go up and down during the day?'; 'Would a goldfish from a tank cope in a rock pool with salty seawater and crashing waves? Why not?'; 'If the rock pool is the animals' home, should we take them out to save them?'
activities.intendedInsight: The animals are not trapped victims — the pool is their home and they are suited to it; the discriminating idea is being able to say HOW at least one animal copes, not just feeling sorry for it.

constraints: Keep the adaptation concrete and singular — one clear coping strategy per animal (limpet clamps, crab hides, anemone withdraws), not a list. Deeper adaptation study is for ages 7–9.
Model and insist on a 'look, don't grab; put creatures back' stance — careful field observation is part of the objective.

Recognition and matching (pointing to the right animal, choosing 'how the limpet survives') check naming and can confirm understanding, but do not by themselves show the child can independently explain a coping behaviour in their own words — include a telling/acting-out step for that.

A static picture and a screen pool are models of real rock-pooling; use real photos/video of a crab scuttling and an anemone's tentacles waving then retracting where possible, since the behaviours themselves are the adaptation evidence.

Connect to prior knowledge of coasts/tides so the changing water level makes sense; the pool is the micro-habitat 'left behind when the tide goes out'. This aligns with the KS1 Y2 micro-habitat requirement.
A 3D lean-in view could add immersion but is not required — the naming and one-adaptation goal needs no spatial reasoning, so don't make it a prerequisite.
Detailed classification (e.g. that a starfish is an invertebrate, not a fish) is seeded only lightly here and belongs to the later classifying topic — don't over-teach it at 5–7.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Both listed sources carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims support the KS1 standard (curriculum context, kept in summary/constraints, not as a method sourceClaim) and the general fact that intertidal animals are adapted to waves/tide (limpet clamping, anemone retraction); they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any particular activity format or medium.

The original framed a tap-to-reveal interactive image as 'ideal' and down-ranked conversation and 3D on catalog-fit grounds; these comparative/necessity judgements are not established by the sources and have been softened to scoped proposals with stated affordances and limits.

Self-audit found no arithmetic, force/motion, or geometric content requiring correction. Biological coping claims (limpet clamping, anemone retraction, crab hiding, starfish not a fish, anemone an animal not a plant) are consistent with the cited Wildlife Trusts claim and standard shore biology.

The 'goldfish would not cope' contrast is a reasonable qualitative counterexample for this age (a freshwater tank fish is not suited to wave-battered saltwater) but is not directly source-supported; keep it conversational rather than as a tested fact.
Tide frequency stated as 'about twice a day on most shores' to avoid overstating a universal — actual tidal pattern varies by location.

probeDeeper: 'When a big wave crashes into the pool, what does the crab do? What does the anemone do?'
'You said the pool changes. What makes the water go up and down during the day?' (tide link)
'A goldfish from a tank — would it cope in a rock pool with crashing waves and changing water? Why not?' (contrast counterexample)
'If the animals live there on purpose, should we take them out to "save" them? Why or why not?'
assess.correctAnswer: It's not right — the animals aren't trapped or dying; a rock pool is a small ocean habitat they are suited to live in. When waves crash and the tide changes the water level, they cope in clever ways: crabs scuttle under rocks or into cracks, anemones pull in their tentacles and close up so they don't dry out, and limpets clamp down tightly onto the rock. The pool changes with the tide, and its creatures are adapted to survive that.

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks rock-pool animals are trapped/stranded and left behind by the sea, struggling to survive
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe the pool as their HOME, not a trap — they live there on purpose and are built for it. Show one coping behaviour (a closed-up anemone) to replace the pity story with adaptation.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — they're stuck and struggling, left behind by the sea
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the animals as stuck/dying; wants to 'rescue' them into the sea

errorPatterns.pattern: Thinks the rock pool stays the same all the time — no sense of the tide changing the water level
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain the tide covers and uncovers the pool twice a day — sometimes crashing waves, sometimes exposed. The animals face big changes and are adapted to them.
errorPatterns.distractor: The rock pool always stays exactly the same
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Second tier: doesn't mention waves/tide changing; treats the pool as a still, unchanging tank

errorPatterns.pattern: Can name rock-pool creatures but cannot say HOW any of them copes with the waves or changing water
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take one named animal and act out its move (clamp like a limpet, close like an anemone, hide like a crab). Attach a coping action to each creature.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Lists crab/anemone/starfish but gives no coping behaviour when asked

responseLevels.gap: Sees the animals as trapped/struggling and the pool as a still tank; no coping behaviours.
responseLevels.full: Describes the rock pool as a small ocean habitat that changes with the tide, and explains how at least one creature copes with waves and changing water levels (clamping, closing up, hiding) — recognising adaptation, not stranding.
responseLevels.partial: Names creatures and says they're a rock-pool habitat, but can't explain how they cope with waves/tides, or misses that the water level changes at all.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child finds a crab and a sea anemone in a rock pool and says: 'They're trapped here — the sea left them behind, so they must be stuck and struggling.' Is that right? Tell me what a rock pool is, and how its animals actually cope when waves crash and the water level goes up and down.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands the habitat says the animals are adapted and names how one copes with waves/tide. A child with the 'stranded and struggling' idea sees the pool as a trap and the animals as victims, with no coping mechanism. The second tier (HOW they cope) is the discriminator: only a child who grasps adaptation can supply a real behaviour, not just sympathy.
